title: THE METADATA YOU DIDN'T KNOW YOU WERE LEAKING
subtitle: YOUR ADDRESS IS ONLY THE BEGINNING.

blocks.text: A PUBLIC LEDGER DOES NOT NEED YOUR NAME TO LEARN YOUR HABITS.
THE TRANSACTION IS ONLY THE FIRST CLUE.

On a transparent blockchain, an address may look anonymous because it is not labeled with a legal name. But the ledger preserves relationships: which outputs were created, which were later spent, how much moved and when activity occurred. The result is not merely a list of payments. It is a graph.

Once one point in that graph becomes associated with a person, exchange, merchant or service, surrounding activity can become easier to interpret. The blockchain does not need to know who you are at the moment a transaction is mined. It can wait for someone to connect the dots later.
PSEUDONYMOUS DOES NOT MEAN UNLINKABLE.
WHAT A TRANSPARENT LEDGER CAN PRESERVE

Transparent Zcash transactions have essentially the same privacy properties as Bitcoin. Inputs, outputs and amounts are public. That can expose balances, payment sizes, timing and transaction relationships. Repeated activity can add structure to the picture even when no single transaction tells the whole story.

Outside information can make that graph more revealing. An exchange may know the identity behind a withdrawal. A merchant may know who paid an invoice. A public donation address may identify its owner. Once an address is attributed, historical transactions remain available for analysis.
TIMING IS METADATA TOO

Cryptographic privacy does not make every surrounding signal disappear. A transaction still happens at a time. It still occupies space on the blockchain. Network observers may have information outside the ledger itself. Wallet behavior, transparent interactions and information voluntarily revealed elsewhere can all create clues.
PRIVACY IS NOT ONE SWITCH. IT IS A STACK.
WHAT A FULLY SHIELDED TRANSFER CHANGES

In a fully shielded Zcash transfer, protected sender and recipient addresses and the transferred amount are not disclosed on the public blockchain. Consensus instead works with commitments, nullifiers, encrypted note data and zero-knowledge proofs. The network can validate the state transition without publishing the ordinary payment graph.

That is a major change in what chain analysis can directly observe. Instead of a visible arrow saying one public address paid another public address a visible amount, the chain sees cryptographic objects that prove the rules were followed.
THE BOUNDARY STILL MATTERS

Moving value between transparent and shielded chain value pools reveals the amount crossing that boundary. The same general caution applies when value moves between distinct shielded pools: pool-crossing amounts can be public even though activity within a shielded pool protects payment details.

This is why privacy can be weakened by recognizable timing and amount patterns. Shielding an exact amount and shortly afterward deshielding the same amount can create an obvious correlation even though the internal shielded activity is not exposed as a transparent transaction graph.
NETWORK PRIVACY IS A DIFFERENT LAYER

Zcash's shielded protocol protects transaction information on the blockchain. It does not automatically guarantee that an internet observer cannot see network metadata. Wallets can add protections at this layer. Zodl, for example, documents Tor support and warns that external services such as price-data providers may otherwise see a user's IP address.
HIDE THE PAYMENT GRAPH. THEN REMEMBER THE NETWORK AROUND IT.
THE DIFFERENCE IN ONE LINE.
THE MOST DANGEROUS METADATA IS OFTEN THE DATA YOU DID NOT REALIZE YOU WERE PUBLISHING.
